intro: Three problems bring together the phenomena of energy, changes of state and gases from the module. In each one, you decide which phenomena and models apply to the situation.

tasks.title: Solar collector
tasks.source_note: The data is calculated from a model and rounded as in a measurement. It is not the result of a real measurement.
tasks.text:
Students built a solar collector: a shallow black box with a glass plate on top. The box contains $4.00\,\text{kg}$ of water. The collector is turned towards the Sun. According to the meter, the power of the solar radiation is $800\,\text{W/m}^2$, that is, $800\,\text{W}$ for every square metre perpendicular to the direction of the Sun, and the area of the collector in this direction is $0.50\,\text{m}^2$. The water is stirred all the time, and its temperature is measured every $5\,\text{min}$. The air temperature is $20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

| $t\ (\text{min})$ | $T\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ |
|---|---|
| $0$ | $20.0$ |
| $5$ | $24.1$ |
| $10$ | $28.0$ |
| $15$ | $31.6$ |
| $20$ | $35.0$ |
| $25$ | $38.0$ |
| $30$ | $40.9$ |
| $35$ | $43.8$ |
| $40$ | $46.2$ |
| $45$ | $48.5$ |
| $50$ | $50.7$ |
| $55$ | $52.8$ |
| $60$ | $54.7$ |

parts.text: Draw a $(t, T)$ graph of the data and fit a model to the points.

criteria.detail: A smooth, levelling-off curve passes through the points.

parts.text: Determine the power at which the water receives energy from the solar radiation. Justify which part of the graph you use to determine it.

criteria.text: Determines the rate of warming from the start of the measurement and justifies it: when the water is at air temperature, almost no heat is transferred to the surroundings.

criteria.detail: The slope at the start from the tangent or the first points, about $0.8\text{–}0.9\,\text{K/min}$.
$Q = cm\Delta T$ and $P = Q : t$, that is, $P = cm \cdot \dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$
$P \approx 240\,\text{W}$; a value of $220\text{–}250\,\text{W}$ obtained from the starting tangent or from the points of the first $5\text{–}10\,\text{min}$ is accepted.

parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the collector at the start of the measurement, when the water is still at air temperature.

criteria.text: Calculates the radiation power arriving at the collector, $800\,\text{W/m}^2 \cdot 0.50\,\text{m}^2 = 400\,\text{W}$, and the efficiency as the ratio of useful power to incoming power.

criteria.detail: $\eta \approx 0.59$, that is, about $60\,\%$ (using the result of part b)

parts.text: Why does the rise in temperature slow down? Determine the power of the heat loss at $50\,\text{min}$.

criteria.text: Explains that the greater the temperature difference between the water and the air, the more heat is conducted and radiated to the surroundings.
Concludes that the power left for the water decreases, so the temperature rises more and more slowly.
Calculates the loss as the difference between the power received from the Sun and the power left for the water, about $120\,\text{W}$.

parts.text: Evaluate two assumptions you used in parts b–d. In which direction does each one affect the results?

criteria.text: Names the first assumption of the measurement or the model and justifies in which direction it changes the result.
Names the second assumption and justifies in which direction it changes the result.

tasks.title: Pressure cooker
tasks.source_note: The values in the table are measured boiling temperatures of water from data books, rounded.
tasks.text:
The lid of a pressure cooker closes tightly. When the water heats up, the pressure in the cooker rises until the valve starts to let steam out. The valve keeps the pressure in the cooker $80\,\text{kPa}$ higher than the outside air pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$. The air left the cooker with the steam during heating, so there is only water vapour under the lid.

| $p\ (\text{kPa})$ | $T_\text{b}\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ |
|---|---|
| $70.2$ | $90$ |
| $84.6$ | $95$ |
| $101.3$ | $100$ |
| $120.9$ | $105$ |
| $143.4$ | $110$ |
| $169.2$ | $115$ |
| $198.7$ | $120$ |
| $232.3$ | $125$ |

The table gives the boiling temperature $T_\text{b}$ of water at different pressures $p$.

parts.text: What is the temperature of the water in the cooker when the valve lets steam out?

criteria.text: Uses the total pressure in the cooker, $101\,\text{kPa} + 80\,\text{kPa} = 181\,\text{kPa}$, and not just the gauge pressure.
Reads the boiling temperature by interpolating between two values in the table or from a graph drawn from the table.

parts.text: Explain why water boils at a higher temperature in a pressure cooker than in an open pot, and why food cooks faster in it.

criteria.text: Links the boiling temperature to pressure: according to the table, at a higher pressure water boils at a higher temperature.

Explains why pressure matters, for example with the particle model: a vapour bubble stays open only if the pressure of its vapour is equal to the surrounding pressure, and the vapour pressure increases with temperature.
Explains the faster cooking by the higher temperature: heat moves into the food faster and the cooking proceeds faster.

parts.text: The cooker contains $1.50\,\text{kg}$ of water and also potatoes. When the valve hisses, the power of the hob is set to $300\,\text{W}$. Of this, $80\,\%$ is transferred to the contents of the cooker and the rest to the surroundings. The potatoes have already warmed through to the temperature of the cooker. How much water vaporises in $20$ minutes?

criteria.text: Justifies that the pressure and temperature stay constant and the potatoes are already at the temperature of the cooker, so the energy transferred to the contents of the cooker is used to vaporise water.

criteria.detail: $\eta P t = rm$, rearranged: $m = \dfrac{\eta P t}{r}$

parts.text: After cooking, someone opens the lid straight away, even though the pressure has not yet dropped. Explain what happens in the cooker. What fraction of the water vaporises?

criteria.text: The pressure drops to the outside air pressure, so the boiling temperature drops to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
The water is hotter than its boiling temperature, so it boils violently until it has cooled to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Conservation of energy: the heat released as the water cools vaporises part of the water, $c m \Delta T = r m_\text{v}$.
Names the danger (steam and splashing boiling water burn) or an assumption of the calculation (the heat of the potatoes and the cooker is left out).

tasks.title: Diving
tasks.text: A diver is at a depth of $15.0\,\text{m}$ in a lake. There the temperature of the water is $6.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and at the surface it is $20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The atmospheric pressure is $101\,\text{kPa}$. The diver breathes from a tank through a regulator: the regulator supplies air at the same pressure as in the surrounding water.

parts.text: The volume of an air bubble breathed out by the diver is $4.0\,\text{cm}^3$ at the bottom. What is its volume at the surface?

criteria.text: Justifies the model: the amount of air in the bubble stays the same, and the bubble is at the temperature of the surrounding water, so $\dfrac{pV}{T}$ stays constant.
Calculates the pressure at depth: $p = p_0 + \rho g h \approx 248\,\text{kPa}$.

parts.text: At a depth of $15.0\,\text{m}$ the diver fills their lungs with $6.0\,\text{l}$ of air. Why is it dangerous to rise to the surface holding your breath? Justify with a calculation.

criteria.text: Chooses a constant temperature and justifies it: the air in the lungs is at body temperature regardless of depth.
Explains the danger: the lungs cannot expand this much, so the air damages them; while rising you breathe normally and never hold your breath, so that the expanding air can escape from the lungs.

parts.text: The volume of the diver's tank is $12.0\,\text{l}$, and its pressure gauge shows a gauge pressure of $200\,\text{bar}$, where $1\,\text{bar} = 100\,\text{kPa}$. At a depth of $15.0\,\text{m}$ the diver uses $20\,\text{l}$ of air per minute at the pressure of that depth. The ascent is started when the gauge shows $50\,\text{bar}$. Assume that the air is equally warm in the tank and in the lungs. How long can the diver stay at this depth?

criteria.text: Uses the given assumption: when the temperature is the same, the amount of air is proportional to the product of pressure and volume (Boyle's law).
Uses total pressures or justifies why the difference of the gauge pressures, $150\,\text{bar}$, is the same as the difference of the total pressures.
Calculates the volume of usable air at the pressure of the depth, about $725\,\text{l}$.

criteria.detail: For example: at the surface the same air would last about $2.5$ times longer, because at depth the pressure is about $2.5$ times as high.

parts.text: Evaluate two assumptions of the calculation in part c. Is the real time likely to be shorter or longer than the calculated one? How should the result be used?

criteria.detail: The first assumption and the direction of its effect.
The second assumption and the direction of its effect.
The calculated time is only a rough estimate, and some margin is left in the plan.
